---
title: "Introduction to Atomic Layer Processing"
---

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## Learning outcomes
After this chapter you should be able to:

1. Name the four atomic layer processes covered in this book (ALD, MLD, ALE and ASD) and say what each one adds to or removes from a surface in one cycle.
2. Use the core vocabulary of the field precisely: precursor, adsorption, surface vs. substrate, monolayer, self-limiting, and layer.
3. Describe the two independent origins of ALD: molecular layering in the Soviet Union and atomic layer epitaxy in Finland.
4. Explain why the technique's first industrial use was in displays, and what moved it into semiconductor manufacturing.
5. Explain why some of the field's terminology ("epitaxy", "atomic layer") is historically rooted rather than physically accurate.
6. Trace how MLD, ALE and ASD grew out of, or alongside, ALD, and how the four processes now work together.
:::

## What is atomic layer processing? {#sec-what-is-alp}

*Atomic layer processing* is a family of thin-film methods that change a surface in small, repeatable steps. Every member of the family uses the same logic. The surface is exposed to one reactant at a time, with a purge or evacuation in between, and each exposure is a gas–surface reaction that stops by itself [@George2016; @Barry2022]. Repeating this cycle gives control over thickness at the scale of a fraction of a nanometre. The test for whether a given process really behaves this way is set out in @sec-what-makes-ald.

This book covers four processes that apply that logic in different ways:

| Process | What one cycle does | Typical per-cycle quantity | Main chapter |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| **Atomic layer deposition (ALD)** | Adds a fraction of a monolayer of an inorganic film | Growth per cycle (GPC), in Å | Chapter 3 |
| **Molecular layer deposition (MLD)** | Adds a molecular fragment, giving an organic or hybrid film | GPC, in Å | Chapter 4 |
| **Atomic layer etching (ALE)** | Removes a thin, chemically modified layer | Etch per cycle (EPC), in Å | (in preparation) |
| **Area-selective deposition (ASD)** | Adds film on one part of a patterned surface but not another | GPC on each surface, and selectivity | (in preparation) |

: The four atomic layer processes covered in this book. {#tbl-four-processes}

The concepts all four share (saturation, ligands, precursors, thermolysis, surface mechanisms and nucleation) are developed once, in Chapter 2. ALD is the oldest and best understood of the four, so most of the examples there come from ALD, and MLD, ALE and ASD are then treated as variations on the same chemistry.

### ALD is not just slow CVD

ALD is often described as a kind of chemical vapour deposition (CVD), and the hardware is similar: valves, a heated reactor, a substrate holder and a pump. The chemistry is different, though [@Barry2022]. In CVD, the reactants are present together. They can react in the gas phase, at the surface, or anywhere in between, and gas-phase reactions are often useful. In ideal ALD, the precursors never meet in the gas phase, and the film forms only through reactions at the surface. Two consequences follow. A single-source precursor, which carries every element of the film and decomposes to deposit it, cannot work in ALD, because nothing would stop the growth. And the precursors in a two-precursor cycle must be stoichiometrically balanced, so that all the ligands from both are removed by the end of the cycle [@Barry2022].

The comparison below shows the four processes side by side. Step through one cycle to see how the same sequence of dose and purge steps can add, remove, or selectively add material.

```{ojs}
  const rect = (x, y, w, h, fill) => `<rect x="${x}" y="${y}" width="${w}" height="${h}" fill="${fill}"/>`;
  const gas = (n, fill, seed) => d3.range(n).map(i =>
    dot(18 + ((i * 47 + seed * 31) % 165), 24 + ((i * 29 + seed * 13) % 40), fill, 4.5)).join("");
  const frame = (title, body, note) => `<svg width="${W}" height="${H}" viewBox="0 0 ${W} ${H}" style="font: 12px sans-serif; background: #fff; border: 1px solid #CFCFCF; border-radius: 6px; margin: 4px;">
    <text x="8" y="15" font-weight="600">${title}</text>${body}
    <text x="8" y="${H - 5}" font-size="10.5" fill="#4D4D4D">${note}</text></svg>`;
  const adsorbed = s === 1 || s === 2;

  // ALD: precursor saturates the surface, purge, second precursor converts it to film, purge.
  const ald = frame("ALD",
    rect(0, 112, W, 30, grey) +
    (s >= 3 ? rect(0, 104, W, 8, "#000") : "") +
    (adsorbed ? xs.map(x => dot(x, 106, red)).join("") : "") +
    (s === 1 ? gas(6, red, 1) : "") + (s === 3 ? gas(6, "#FFFFFF", 2) : ""),
    s >= 3 ? "Film grows by one GPC" : s >= 1 ? "Precursor saturates the surface" : "Starting surface");

  // MLD: as ALD, but the adsorbed species and the added layer are molecular.
  const mld = frame("MLD",
    rect(0, 112, W, 30, grey) +
    (s >= 3 ? rect(0, 94, W, 18, dark) : "") +
    (adsorbed ? xs.map(x => `<line x1="${x}" y1="112" x2="${x}" y2="94" stroke="${red}" stroke-width="4" stroke-linecap="round"/>`).join("") : "") +
    (s === 1 ? gas(6, red, 3) : "") + (s === 3 ? gas(6, "#FFFFFF", 4) : ""),
    s >= 3 ? "A molecular layer is added" : s >= 1 ? "Organic molecules bind upright" : "Starting surface");

  // ALE: modify the top of the film, purge, remove only the modified layer, purge.
  const top = s >= 3 ? 94 : 88;
  const ale = frame("ALE",
    rect(0, 112, W, 30, grey) + rect(0, top, W, 112 - top, "#000") +
    (adsorbed ? rect(0, 88, W, 6, red) : "") +
    (s === 1 ? gas(6, red, 5) : "") + (s === 3 ? gas(5, "#FFFFFF", 6) + gas(3, red, 7) : ""),
    s >= 3 ? "Film is thinner by one EPC" : s >= 1 ? "Top of the film is modified" : "Film to be etched");

  // ASD: an inhibitor blocks the right-hand (non-growth) surface; growth occurs only on the left.
  const asd = frame("ASD",
    rect(0, 112, half, 30, grey) + rect(half, 112, half, 30, "#E3E3E3") +
    xs.filter(x => x > half).map(x => `<line x1="${x}" y1="112" x2="${x}" y2="101" stroke="#000" stroke-width="1.2"/>` + dot(x, 98, "#FFFFFF", 3)).join("") +
    (s >= 3 ? rect(0, 104, half, 8, "#000") : "") +
    (adsorbed ? xs.filter(x => x < half).map(x => dot(x, 106, red)).join("") : "") +
    (s === 1 ? gas(6, red, 8) : "") + (s === 3 ? gas(6, "#FFFFFF", 9) : ""),
    s >= 3 ? "Film grows only where wanted" : s >= 1 ? "Inhibitor blocks the right side" : "Growth vs. non-growth surface");

  const div = document.createElement("div");
  div.style.cssText = "display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(2, auto); justify-content: center;";
  div.innerHTML = ald + mld + ale + asd;
  return div;
}
```

## Vocabulary {#sec-vocabulary}

Many terms in this field are used loosely, and some have been borrowed from other disciplines. Using them precisely makes the chemistry easier to discuss [@Barry2022]. This book uses the following definitions.

Precursor
: Any volatile compound that takes part in the surface chemistry of the process. "Reactant" is chemically correct but too general. "Co-reactant" and "co-precursor" are avoided here, because the prefix *co-* implies that two compounds are dosed at the same time, which is exactly what an atomic layer process does not do. In a two-precursor process, this book refers to the *first* and *second* precursor [@Barry2022].

Adsorption
: The general term for a molecule binding to a surface. It covers **chemisorption**, which involves a change in bonding (for example, loss of a ligand as a volatile by-product) and is hard to reverse, and **physisorption**, a weak and easily reversed interaction that is often the first step towards chemisorption. "Adsorption" is the safe word to use until the mechanism is known [@Barry2022].

Substrate and surface
: The *substrate* is the material on which deposition starts, a term borrowed from microelectronics. Once the substrate is covered, the process continues on the growing film, which is the *surface*. The precursor and the surface together make up the thermodynamic system, so when the surface changes from substrate to film, the chemistry can change too [@Barry2022]. This is the root of the nucleation effects discussed in @sec-surfaces, and of area-selective deposition.

Monolayer
: A layer of adsorbed species after which the surface will not accept any more. It does not have to be densely packed: the size of the precursor, the number of reactive sites and the surface roughness all limit how full it is [@Barry2022].

Self-limiting
: The defining property of an atomic layer process. Once the monolayer forms, adsorption stops, and the layer stays in place until the next reaction. The monolayer need not be thermodynamically stable; it is enough that it is kinetically stable, i.e. that it lasts long enough for the next step [@Barry2022].

Layer
: Used in at least three senses: an adsorbed monolayer, the result of one half-reaction, and one full layer of the target material. Most ALD processes deposit less than one layer of the target material per cycle, so several cycles contribute to a single layer of film. Always say which kind of layer you mean [@Barry2022].

Growth per cycle (GPC) and etch per cycle (EPC)
: The thickness added (GPC) or removed (EPC) by one complete cycle. In this book both are reported in Å, never Å/cycle.

Growth surface and non-growth surface
: In area-selective deposition, the part of a patterned surface where film is wanted and the part where it is not [@Parsons2020].

## History of atomic layer deposition {#sec-history-ald}

ALD is the oldest of the four processes, and its history is the best documented. It is also unusual: the technique was invented twice, in two countries, by people who did not know of each other's work.

### The dual history of atomic layer deposition

ALD was discovered independently at least twice, under different names [@Ahvenniemi2017; @Puurunen2014; @Barry2022]:

- **Molecular layering (ML)**, developed in Leningrad from the 1960s by V. B. Aleskovskii and his student S. I. Kol'tsov [@Malygin2015; @Barry2022].
- **Atomic layer epitaxy (ALE)**, developed in Finland from 1974 by Tuomo Suntola and co-workers [@Puurunen2014].

Both rest on the principle from @sec-what-makes-ald: repeated, separate, saturating gas–solid reactions. They reached it from opposite directions, though, and each lineage left its mark on how ALD is thought about today.

#### Molecular layering: a chemical question

The Leningrad work started from a question about solids, not films. In his 1952 doctoral thesis at the Leningrad Technological Institute, Aleskovskii proposed what he called the "matrix" or "framework" hypothesis [@Malygin2015; @Barry2022]. A solid framework carries a stoichiometric number of reactive surface sites relative to its bulk atoms. If those sites are reacted with a suitable chemical, the result is a new surface that again carries a stoichiometric number of sites. The cyclical logic of ALD is already present in this idea: each reaction regenerates the conditions for the next [@Barry2022].

The method followed over the next two decades [@Barry2022]:

- **1963:** first report of molecular layering, in the Russian literature.
- **1965:** first full paper, by Aleskovskii in *J. Appl. Chem. USSR*.
- **1971:** Kol'tsov's doctoral dissertation, which contains much of what would now be called the chemical conceptualization of ALD. In the same year, Kol'tsov and Aleskovskii applied for a patent titled "The Principles of Synthesis of Solids". It was declined.

Throughout, molecular layering was framed as surface chemistry: how to change a material's surface by chemical means, producing different kinds of surfaces and different ratios of bulk atoms to surface sites [@Barry2022]. It reached few readers outside the USSR. A detailed English-language account of Aleskovskii and Kol'tsov's work only appeared in 2015 [@Malygin2015].

#### Atomic layer epitaxy: an engineering answer

In 1974, the Finnish medical-technology company Instrumentarium asked Suntola, a young physicist, to lead a new R&D effort. He chose thin-film electroluminescent (EL) displays. These need very thin, uniform, pinhole-free films with high dielectric strength, over large areas. The original target was high-quality **polycrystalline ZnS** for EL panels [@Puurunen2014].

Suntola and Jorma Antson filed the patent "Method for Producing Compound Thin Films" in 1974 [@Puurunen2014; @Barry2022]. Where molecular layering asked a chemical question, ALE was engineered from the start as an industrial solution for making devices, and it focused on the physics and engineering of depositing and characterizing films [@Barry2022]. The patent shows this. It contains detailed technical drawings of a reactor, and the ALE work laid the technical foundations of concepts that are now active research areas in their own right, including area-selective ALD and spatial ALD [@Barry2022].

In 1977 the team moved to Lohja Corporation, which built an electronics factory in Espoo in 1984 to make ALE-grown ZnS:Mn displays. This was the first industrial use of the technique. Display modules from the line served in the departure hall of Helsinki-Vantaa airport for about two decades. Suntola's display work also explains why early ALD concentrated on chalcogenides (sulfides and selenides); oxides and nitrides came to the fore in the 1990s [@Barry2022].

#### A missed connection

The two lineages developed without collaboration, and very likely without knowledge of each other. Given how differently they were framed, that is not surprising: one was about the chemistry of a surface relative to the bulk, the other about the engineering of thin-film devices [@Barry2022].

They did come close to meeting. In the late 1970s, Suntola defended his patent application in Moscow, and the patent was granted in the Soviet jurisdiction. The examiners did not raise molecular layering as prior art, and an early chance to join the two bodies of work was missed [@Barry2022]. A deliberate effort to bring the two histories together began only in 2004, and it led to the VPHA (see below) [@Barry2022; @Ahvenniemi2017]. Riikka Puurunen can be credited with bringing the early Russian contributions to the forefront [@Barry2022].

| | Molecular layering | Atomic layer epitaxy |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Where | Leningrad Technological Institute, USSR | Instrumentarium, then Lohja, Finland |
| Key people | V. B. Aleskovskii, S. I. Kol'tsov | T. Suntola, J. Antson |
| Origin | 1952 "framework" hypothesis; first reports 1963–1965 | 1974 patent application |
| Framing | Chemistry: modifying the surface of a solid | Engineering: depositing films for devices |
| Patent | 1971 application declined | Granted, including in the USSR |
| Reach | Published mainly in Russian | International patents and conferences |

: The two origins of ALD compared [@Malygin2015; @Puurunen2014; @Barry2022]. {#tbl-origins}

The way we draw ALD has changed with the field. Kol'tsov's 1971 thesis pictured the growing surface as a regular lattice of atomic points, one layer added per cycle. Modern depictions, such as Puurunen's, show bulky chemisorbed precursor fragments and the complexity of the surface reactions [@Barry2022]. Simulation 3.1 in @sec-tma-model sits between the two: a cartoon, but one that shows steric shielding and more than one adsorbed species.

#### What's in a name

The ZnS films were polycrystalline, so "epitaxy" was never strictly correct. As the materials list grew to amorphous oxides and nitrides, the name became a liability. The term "atomic layer deposition" was first used around 1990 and became the common name in the mid-1990s. The same mismatch between name and physics applies to "atomic layer", since a cycle deposits a fraction of a monolayer (@sec-what-makes-ald).

### From displays to microchips

Finland stayed the centre of the field through the 1980s and 1990s:

- Lauri Niinistö started ALD process research at the Helsinki University of Technology in 1982. Espoo hosted the first ALE symposium in 1984 and the first international ALE symposium in 1990.
- Neste founded Microchemistry (Mikrokemia) in Espoo in 1987, with Suntola leading it, to apply ALD to catalysts and solar cells. Microchemistry also built some of the first commercial ALD reactors, the F120 series.
- Markku Leskelä and Mikko Ritala's group at the University of Helsinki developed much of the precursor chemistry, in a decades-long partnership with the reactor makers.

The turning point came in 1999, when ASM International (Netherlands) bought Microchemistry and refocused it on semiconductors. By then, the industry could see that the SiO~2~ gate dielectric would have to be replaced, and ALD could deposit the ultrathin high-k films needed. In 2007, Intel shipped 45 nm processors whose transistors used a hafnium-based high-k gate dielectric deposited by ALD, the first fundamental change to the CMOS transistor in four decades. ALD is now routine in logic, DRAM and 3D NAND manufacturing.

### A field with a conference and a name

The community first met in Finland: a symposium on atomic layer epitaxy was held in Espoo in 1984, followed by four international ALE symposia between 1990 and 1996, in Finland, the USA, Japan and Austria [@AtomicLimits2024]. The first AVS conference on ALD was held in Monterey, California, in 2001, chaired by Steven George; the second was held in Seoul in 2002 [@Parsons2013]. Since then the meeting has run every year, rotating between the United States, Europe and Asia, and since 2015 it has been held jointly with the International Atomic Layer Etching Workshop [@AtomicLimits2024]. The 2020 and 2021 meetings were virtual. The 2024 meeting in Helsinki marked 50 years since the first ALE patent, and the 2026 meeting in Tampa, Florida, was the 26th [@AtomicLimits2024; @AVS2026]. Suntola received the Millennium Technology Prize for ALD in 2018.

The map below includes every in-person meeting in the series; choose the North America or East Asia view to separate the clusters.

### Recovering the history

Because the two lineages developed in isolation, the early literature is scattered across languages and journals. An effort to join the two histories began in 2004 [@Barry2022]. It led to the **Virtual Project on the History of ALD** (VPHA), launched in July 2013 as an open, volunteer effort to make the early work visible [@Ahvenniemi2017]. Participants read and discussed early publications from both lineages. The result was a recommended reading list, presented at the ALD 2016 conference in Dublin and published the following year with dozens of co-authors [@Ahvenniemi2017]. The VPHA has since closed, but the reading list remains the best entry point to the early literature.

## History of molecular layer deposition {#sec-history-mld}

MLD applies the ALD cycle to organic molecules. Instead of adding a fraction of a monolayer of an inorganic solid, each cycle adds a molecular fragment, giving a purely organic or a hybrid organic–inorganic film [@Sundberg2014].

### Organic polymers, one layer at a time

The term "molecular layer deposition" and the first experiments with organic molecules came from Tetsuzo Yoshimura and co-workers at Fujitsu in 1991 [@Yoshimura1991; @Sundberg2014]. They wanted to build polymer films molecule by molecule, so that the chain structure could be controlled, and they made polyimide films by alternating exposures of pyromellitic dianhydride and an aromatic diamine. Each exposure saturated within about a minute and added roughly 5 Å, close to the size of one molecule, and fifteen exposures gave a film about 100 Å thick [@Yoshimura1991]. Through the 1990s and early 2000s, MLD remained a niche method for organic polymers such as polyimides and polyamides [@Sundberg2014].

### The hybrid turn

MLD became a partner to ALD when metal precursors were combined with organic linkers. In 2008, the George group at the University of Colorado reported "alucone" films grown from trimethylaluminum and ethylene glycol [@Dameron2008]. Alucones, and the related zincones, titanicones and other "metalcones", use the familiar ALD metal precursors with diols and other bifunctional organics as the second precursor. Because the chemistry is shared, ALD and MLD cycles can be mixed in one process to make nanolaminates and alloys with tunable properties [@Sundberg2014]. MLD processes are covered in Chapter 4 (@sec-mld-processes) and in Chapter 8 of @Barry2022.

### A different failure mode

MLD brought a problem with no simple ALD analogue. A bifunctional molecule can react with the surface at both ends, a "double reaction", which uses up two sites and leaves no functional group for the next step. This is a recurring theme in MLD process development [@Sundberg2014].

## History of atomic layer etching {#sec-history-ale}

ALE is the subtractive counterpart of ALD. A cycle has a *modification* step, which creates a thin reactive layer at the surface, and a *removal* step, which takes away only that layer [@Kanarik2015].

### A patent, then a first wave

As with ALD, the first report on ALE was a patent. Max Yoder of the US Office of Naval Research filed "Atomic layer etching" in 1987, and it was granted in 1988 [@Yoder1988; @Kanarik2015]. The patent described removing a single atomic layer from diamond: nitrogen dioxide was adsorbed on the surface and then exposed to pulses of ions from a noble-gas and hydrogen plasma, with purges in between. Work in Japan followed. In 1990, Yasuhiro Horiike described "digital" etching and deposition, in which each step of a process is separated in time so that it can be controlled at the atomic scale [@Horiike1990]. Silicon and gallium arsenide were etched using two-step cycles of chlorine adsorption and ion bombardment. This first wave of research ran through the 1990s [@Fischer2021].

### A second wave, driven by device scaling

Interest returned in the mid-2010s, when feature sizes below 10 nm made continuous plasma etching hard to control [@Fischer2021]. Kanarik and co-workers at Lam Research published an overview in 2015 that set out the definitions now in common use: a process is ALE if it is divided into separate steps and at least one step is as self-limiting as possible [@Kanarik2015]. The same year, the ALE community began meeting jointly with the ALD conference (@sec-history-ald).

### Thermal ALE: ALD in reverse

The early ALE processes used ions for the removal step, which makes them directional (anisotropic). In 2015, Younghee Lee and Steven George reported a purely thermal ALE of Al~2~O~3~ [@Lee2015]. Hydrogen fluoride converts the surface to AlF~3~, and tin(II) acetylacetonate then removes the fluoride through ligand exchange, producing volatile products. Because no ions are used, the etch is isotropic. George and Lee described thermal ALE as the reverse of ALD [@George2016], and its chemistry (ligand exchange, volatility, thermal stability of the products) is the same precursor chemistry that underlies ALD. Chapter 9 of @Barry2022 works through several of these mechanisms.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Two meanings of "ALE"
In the older literature, "ALE" means atomic layer *epitaxy*, Suntola's original name for ALD (@sec-history-ald). From the 2010s, "ALE" almost always means atomic layer *etching*; "ALEt" is sometimes used to avoid confusion. Check the date and context when you meet the acronym in a paper.
:::

## History of area-selective deposition {#sec-history-asd}

Area-selective deposition grows a film on one part of a patterned surface (the growth surface) but not on another (the non-growth surface). It is "bottom-up" patterning: the pattern on the substrate decides where the film goes, rather than lithography and etching [@Parsons2020].

### Selectivity is older than ALD in the fab

Selective deposition was used in semiconductor processing well before area-selective ALD. Selective epitaxy was already routine, and in the 1980s selective CVD of tungsten from WF~6~ and H~2~ was developed to fill contact holes: tungsten grows on silicon and metals, but nucleates slowly on SiO~2~ [@Gladfelter1993]. Selectivity was always eventually lost as stray nuclei formed on the oxide. In 1993, Wayne Gladfelter reviewed selective metal CVD and proposed a working definition of selectivity based on the relative rates of nucleation on the growth and non-growth surfaces [@Gladfelter1993], an idea that still underlies how selectivity is measured.

### Blocking the surface

Because ALD depends on reactive sites at the surface, it is a natural fit for selective deposition: remove the sites, and growth should not start. In 2004, Rong Chen, Stacey Bent and co-workers at Stanford showed that a self-assembled monolayer (SAM) of octadecyltrichlorosilane could block HfO~2~ ALD, so that the film grew only on the regions left uncovered [@Chen2004]. Using SAMs and, later, polymers and small-molecule inhibitors to deactivate the non-growth surface became one of the main strategies for ASD [@Mackus2019; @Parsons2020].

### From a problem to a method

For most of ALD's history, a delay in nucleation on some substrates was a nuisance to be overcome. For ASD, that same delay is the effect being exploited: a long nucleation delay on the non-growth surface and immediate growth on the growth surface give a window of selective growth [@Parsons2020]. The industrial pull came from patterning. As features shrink, aligning each new layer to the one below by lithography becomes harder, and a film that places itself by surface chemistry is "self-aligned" [@Mackus2019; @Parsons2020].

### A community forms

ASD gained its own meeting in 2016, when the first Area Selective Deposition workshop was held at imec in Leuven. The second followed in Eindhoven in 2017 and the third in Raleigh, North Carolina, in 2018 [@AtomicLimits2017]. Strategies have broadened since then: inhibitors dosed in the vapour phase as part of an ABC cycle, area *activation* rather than deactivation, and periodic etch-back steps that remove stray nuclei from the non-growth surface [@Mackus2019; @Parsons2020].

## Atomic layer processing today {#sec-convergence}

The four processes began separately but are now increasingly used together [@George2016; @Parsons2020]:

- **ALD and ALE** share precursor chemistry, and thermal ALE is ALD in reverse. Since 2015 the two communities have met at the same conference.
- **ALD and MLD** use the same metal precursors, and their cycles can be combined in one film.
- **ASD and ALE** are combined in supercycles: a few ALD cycles build film selectively, then a short etch removes the stray nuclei that have formed on the non-growth surface, resetting the selectivity [@Mackus2019].

The timeline below brings together the milestones from all four histories.

::: {.sim-box}
[Interactive 1.3: Four histories on one timeline]{.sim-title}

## Check your understanding

::: {.quiz}
Why did molecular layering remain largely unknown outside the USSR until the 2010s?

- [ ] It used chemistry that did not work outside a laboratory.
- [x] It was published mainly in Russian and developed with little contact with Western thin-film researchers.
- [ ] It was classified military research until 2013.
- [ ] It was a later copy of atomic layer epitaxy.

::: {.explanation}
Molecular layering predates ALE, so it was not a copy. The main barrier was language and isolation, which is exactly what the VPHA set out to address [@Ahvenniemi2017; @Malygin2015].
:::
:::

::: {.quiz}
What was the first industrial application of ALD?

- [ ] High-k gate dielectrics in microprocessors
- [ ] Copper diffusion barriers
- [x] ZnS-based thin-film electroluminescent displays
- [ ] Catalyst supports

::: {.explanation}
ALE was invented to make the thin, uniform, high-breakdown-strength films that EL displays need, and Lohja began producing displays in Espoo in the 1980s. Semiconductor use came about two decades later [@Puurunen2014].
:::
:::

::: {.quiz}
Why is "atomic layer epitaxy" a misleading name, even for Suntola's original ZnS films?

- [x] The films were polycrystalline, not epitaxial, and each cycle deposits less than one atomic layer.
- [ ] The films were grown from liquid precursors.
- [ ] ZnS cannot be grown epitaxially.
- [ ] The process was plasma-enhanced.

::: {.explanation}
"Epitaxy" means growth with a crystallographic relationship to the substrate, which the polycrystalline ZnS films did not have [@Puurunen2014]. "Atomic layer" overstates what one cycle deposits (@sec-what-makes-ald). Both terms record the technique's history rather than its physics.
:::
:::

::: {.quiz}
A colleague describes HfO~2~ as being deposited "using TDMAH and the co-reactant water". How would this book describe the same process?

- [ ] TDMAH is the precursor and water is the reactant.
- [x] TDMAH and water are the first and second precursors.
- [ ] Water is the co-precursor, because it is dosed with TDMAH.
- [ ] TDMAH is a single-source precursor.

::: {.explanation}
Any volatile compound that takes part in the surface chemistry is a precursor. The prefix *co-* implies simultaneous dosing, which is exactly what ALD avoids (@sec-vocabulary).
:::
:::

::: {.quiz}
What made thermal ALE a natural extension of ALD chemistry?

- [ ] It uses the same ion sources as plasma ALD.
- [x] Its removal step is a ligand-exchange reaction that forms volatile metal complexes, the same precursor chemistry that governs ALD.
- [ ] It deposits and etches in the same cycle.
- [ ] It works only on Al~2~O~3~ grown by ALD.

::: {.explanation}
In thermal ALE of Al~2~O~3~, HF fluorinates the surface and a metal precursor removes the fluoride by ligand exchange. Whether etching happens depends on whether the products are stable and volatile, which is a precursor-chemistry question [@Lee2015; @George2016].
:::
:::

::: {.quiz}
Why is a nucleation delay useful in area-selective deposition, when it is a problem in most ALD processes?

- [ ] It increases the GPC on the growth surface.
- [ ] It removes the need for a purge step.
- [x] A long delay on the non-growth surface, with prompt growth on the growth surface, gives a window of cycles in which film forms only where it is wanted.
- [ ] It makes the film epitaxial.

::: {.explanation}
ASD exploits the difference in nucleation between two surfaces. Selectivity is lost once nuclei build up on the non-growth surface, which is why etch-back steps are sometimes added [@Gladfelter1993; @Parsons2020].
:::
:::

## Further reading

- @Barry2022, Chapter 1: an introduction to ALD chemistry, including the history of both lineages.
- @Puurunen2014: the story of ALE as told by its inventor, written for the 40th anniversary. Open access.
- @Malygin2015: the first detailed English-language account of molecular layering and of Aleskovskii and Kol'tsov.
- @Ahvenniemi2017: the VPHA reading list of early publications from both lineages. Open access.
- @Parsons2013: how the ALD community and its conference grew within the AVS.
- @Sundberg2014: a review of hybrid ALD/MLD materials, including the history of MLD. Open access.
- @Kanarik2015: an overview of ALE in the semiconductor industry, with its history and definitions.
- @Fischer2021: a review of thermal ALE.
- @Parsons2020: the fundamentals and applications of area-selective deposition, including its history.
